In this chapter

Construct and read an ROC curve

Chapter 1 imposed a cut-off of 14 ng/L and moved on. That number did more work than any other decision in this course. Change it and every measure changes with it.

title: Thresholds and the ROC Curve
text:
2 Two overlapping distributions
The reason a perfect threshold does not exist is visible in the raw data. Patients with and without infarction have different troponin distributions — but the distributions overlap.








Figure 1: Troponin on a log scale, by final diagnosis. Any vertical line drawn through this figure cuts through both distributions: some diseased patients fall to its left, some healthy patients to its right.











Why overlap is unavoidable



If the two distributions separated cleanly, a threshold in the gap would give 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity, and diagnosis would be a solved problem. Biological variation, assay imprecision and heterogeneous disease guarantee the overlap. Choosing a threshold means choosing where in the overlap to stand.

text:
3 Sweeping the cut-off

cutoffs <- c(5, 10, 14, 20, 30, 50, 100)

sweep <- t(sapply(cutoffs, function(k) {

  mk <- dtx_measures(tk)
  c(cutoff = k, TP = tk$tp, FP = tk$fp, FN = tk$fn, TN = tk$tn,
    sensitivity = round(mk$sensitivity, 3),
    specificity = round(mk$specificity, 3),
    PPV = round(mk$ppv, 3))
}))

title: Thresholds and the ROC Curve
text:
4 The ROC curve
Plot the true positive rate against the false positive rate at every possible cut-off, and you get the receiver operating characteristic curve.








Figure 2: Empirical ROC curve for troponin. Each point is one possible threshold. The diagonal is what an uninformative test would produce.





The curve is a summary of the whole family of tests you could build from one measurement. Moving along it towards the upper right buys sensitivity with specificity; moving down-left does the reverse.

title: Thresholds and the ROC Curve
text:
5 Area under the curve

roc <- dtx_roc(cohort$troponin_ng_L, cohort$mi_confirmed)
auc <- dtx_auc(roc)
round(auc, 3)

[1] 0.953


The AUC here is 0.953. Its interpretation is specific and often misquoted: it is the probability that a randomly chosen diseased patient has a higher test value than a randomly chosen patient without the disease (Hanley and McNeil 1982).






What AUC does not tell you




It is not accuracy. It is threshold-independent, so it says nothing about how the test performs at the cut-off you will actually use.
It ignores clinical cost. Two tests with identical AUC can differ completely in the region of the curve that matters for your decision.
It ignores prevalence. A test with an excellent AUC can still have a hopeless PPV in a low-prevalence setting, as Chapter 3 showed.

Report the AUC. Then report sensitivity, specificity and predictive values at the threshold you intend to use, which is the number a clinician can act on.

title: Thresholds and the ROC Curve
text:
6 Choosing a threshold honestly
The Youden index (\(J = \text{sensitivity} + \text{specificity} - 1\)) picks the point furthest above the diagonal.

youden <- sapply(sort(unique(cohort$troponin_ng_L)), function(k) {
  mk <- dtx_measures(dtx_table(cohort$troponin_ng_L >= k, cohort$mi_confirmed))
  mk$sensitivity + mk$specificity - 1
})
best <- sort(unique(cohort$troponin_ng_L))[which.max(youden)]
best

[1] 21.9


Youden treats a false negative and a false positive as equally bad. In acute coronary syndrome they are not remotely equal: a missed infarction may be fatal, while a false positive costs an admission and an angiogram. Weight the errors and the optimum moves.








Figure 3: Expected cost across candidate thresholds under three assumptions about how much worse a missed infarction is than a false alarm. The optimum shifts markedly to the left as the penalty for missing disease rises.






The rule-out strategy
This is why emergency departments run troponin as a rule-out test with a low threshold, accepting many false positives to drive false negatives towards zero. The threshold encodes a value judgement about which error the department is willing to make. Making that judgement explicit is better practice than inheriting a cut-off from the assay insert.

title: Thresholds and the ROC Curve
text:
7 Check yourself

Test A has an AUC of 0.91; test B has an AUC of 0.88. Which conclusion is justified?

Test A is the better choice for this clinical problem
Test A is more accurate at every threshold
Test A discriminates better on average, but B may still be preferable at the threshold you need
Test A has a higher positive predictive value


AUC averages across all thresholds. ROC curves can cross, so test B may well dominate in the high-sensitivity region where a rule-out test operates. And neither AUC says anything about predictive value, which depends on prevalence.



You lower the troponin threshold from 14 ng/L to 5 ng/L. Which pair of changes follows necessarily?

Sensitivity rises and specificity rises
Sensitivity rises and specificity falls
Sensitivity falls and specificity rises
Sensitivity is unchanged and PPV rises


A lower threshold calls more patients positive. More diseased patients are caught, so sensitivity rises; more healthy patients are wrongly flagged, so specificity falls. Compare the rows for 5 and 14 in the sweep table above and you can watch it happen.

title: Predictive Values and Prevalence
text:
In this chapter

Calculate positive and negative predictive value
Show how both change with prevalence while sensitivity and specificity do not
Apply Bayes’ theorem using likelihood ratios
Explain why a good test can still produce mostly false alarms


Chapter 2 read the table down its columns. Predictive values read it across the rows — starting from the result the patient actually has.
\[
\text{PPV} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}
\qquad\qquad
\text{NPV} = \frac{TN}{TN + FN}
\]

ppv <- tab$tp / (tab$tp + tab$fp)
npv <- tab$tn / (tab$tn + tab$fn)

c(ppv = round(ppv, 3), npv = round(npv, 3))

  ppv   npv 
0.333 0.992 


In our cohort, a positive troponin carries a 33.3% probability of a confirmed infarction, and a negative one leaves a 0.8% residual probability.

title: Predictive Values and Prevalence
text:
2 The prevalence trap
Here is the result that surprises people. Hold the test constant — same assay, same threshold, same sensitivity of 96.1% and specificity of 71.7% — and vary only how common the disease is.








Figure 1: Predictive values across the plausible range of prevalence, with the test itself held fixed. The dashed line marks our cohort. PPV collapses as disease becomes rare; NPV barely moves.

Applied as a population screen, this same test produces roughly 147 false alarms for every genuine case found. Nothing about the assay has deteriorated. The test is fine; the deployment is wrong.

The clinical consequence
This is the argument against unfocused testing. Ordering a troponin on a patient with a very low pre-test probability does not produce information — it produces a result that is more likely to be wrong than right, along with the admission, the anticoagulation and the angiogram that follow from it.

title: Predictive Values and Prevalence
Predictive Values and Prevalence
text:
4 Likelihood ratios: the portable version
Predictive values are specific to the population they were measured in, which makes them awkward to carry between settings. Likelihood ratios solve this. They describe the test, like sensitivity and specificity, but combine directly with any pre-test probability (Deeks and Altman 2004).
\[
LR^+ = \frac{\text{Sensitivity}}{1 - \text{Specificity}}
\qquad\qquad
LR^- = \frac{1 - \text{Sensitivity}}{\text{Specificity}}
\]

lr_pos <- sn / (1 - sp)
lr_neg <- (1 - sn) / sp
c(LR_positive = round(lr_pos, 2), LR_negative = round(lr_neg, 3))

LR_positive LR_negative 
      3.400       0.054 


Apply them in odds, then convert back:
\[
\text{post-test odds} = \text{pre-test odds} \times LR
\]

1pre  <- 0.13
2odds_pre  <- pre / (1 - pre)
3odds_post <- odds_pre * lr_pos
4post <- odds_post / (1 + odds_post)

round(c(pre_test = pre, post_test = post), 3)

title: Predictive Values and Prevalence
text:
5 Check yourself

A test with sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.99 is used to screen for a condition affecting 1 in 10,000 people. A patient tests positive. Roughly what is the probability they have the condition?

About 99%
About 50%
About 1%
About 0.01%


In 1,000,000 people: 100 have the condition and 99 test positive. Of the 999,900 without it, about 9,999 test positive. So 99 out of roughly 10,098 positives are genuine — about 1%. An excellent test, applied to a rare condition, still yields a hundred false alarms per true case. Set the slider above to 0.0001 and watch it happen.



A patient’s pre-test probability is 20%. A test with a positive likelihood ratio of 8 comes back positive. The post-test probability is closest to:

28%
40%
67%
80%


Pre-test odds = 0.2/0.8 = 0.25. Post-test odds = 0.25 × 8 = 2. Probability = 2/(1+2) = 0.67. Note that you cannot simply multiply the probability by the likelihood ratio — 20% × 8 would give 160%, which is why the conversion to odds is not optional.

title: Case Studies
text:
In this chapter

Apply likelihood ratios to individual patients with different pre-test probabilities
Recognise when a test result should not change management
Check whether accuracy holds up in clinically relevant subgroups
Everything so far has described populations. Clinical work happens one patient at a time. These three attend the same department on the same evening and all have their troponin measured with the same assay, whose likelihood ratios we established in Chapter 3:
Positive LR = 3.4    Negative LR = 0.054

title: Case Studies
section: 1 Does accuracy hold in every subgroup?
text:
1 Does accuracy hold in every subgroup?
Sensitivity and specificity are stable across prevalence, but not necessarily across case mix. Worth checking directly.

subgroup <- function(rows, label) {
  d <- cohort[rows, ]
  t <- dtx_table(d$test_positive, d$mi_confirmed)
  s <- dtx_measures(t)
  data.frame(Subgroup = label, n = t$n,
             Prevalence = pct(s$prevalence),
             Sensitivity = pct(s$sensitivity),
             Specificity = pct(s$specificity),
             PPV = pct(s$ppv))
}

results <- rbind(
  subgroup(rep(TRUE, nrow(cohort)),          "All patients"),
  subgroup(cohort$sex == "F",                "Women"),
  subgroup(cohort$sex == "M",                "Men"),
  subgroup(cohort$hours_since_onset < 3,     "Presenting < 3 h"),
  subgroup(cohort$hours_since_onset >= 3,    "Presenting >= 3 h"),
  subgroup(cohort$age < 60,                  "Age under 60"),
  subgroup(cohort$age >= 60,                 "Age 60 and over")
)

How to read this table





Look across the prevalence column, then across sensitivity and specificity. The prevalence differences do not drag sensitivity and specificity with them — that is the independence from Chapter 2, visible in real numbers. PPV, by contrast, tracks prevalence closely.
Where sensitivity does differ between subgroups, suspect a genuine biological difference in the test’s behaviour rather than a prevalence effect. Early presentation is the classic example: troponin needs time to rise, so tests taken within a few hours of symptom onset genuinely miss more infarctions. Small subgroups also produce unstable estimates, so check the denominators before concluding anything.

title: Case Studies
text:
3 Check yourself

Case C has a pre-test probability of 95% and a negative troponin. What is the correct action?

Discharge him, since the test was negative
Repeat the troponin in six hours before deciding
Proceed to reperfusion on the basis of the ECG and history
Order a d-dimer instead


His post-test probability remains around 80%, far above any threshold for treatment, and troponin may not yet have risen in an infarct of 40 minutes’ duration. A test that cannot move the patient across a decision threshold should not delay treatment.



In the subgroup table, PPV differs markedly between women and men while sensitivity is similar. The most likely explanation is:

The assay performs less well in women
The prevalence of confirmed infarction differs between the two groups
The reference standard was applied inconsistently
The sample size is too small to interpret


PPV depends on prevalence; sensitivity does not. When sensitivity and specificity are stable but PPV moves, prevalence is the first explanation to consider. A genuine difference in assay performance would show up in sensitivity or specificity as well.

title: Diagnostic Test Accuracy
text:
The clinical question
A 58-year-old man. Chest pain. Troponin 22 ng/L, above the cut-off.

Does he have a myocardial infarction?


The test does not answer this. It shifts a probability.
How far, and from where, is the whole subject.

title: Diagnostic Test Accuracy
text:
What this means in practice


A positive troponin in the coronary care unit is strong evidence
The same result in a low-risk outpatient is more likely a false alarm
Ordering a test on a patient with a very low pre-test probability generates noise, not information
The threshold is a value judgement about which error you prefer

title: Diagnostic Test Accuracy
text:
Likelihood ratios travel
\[\text{post-test odds} = \text{pre-test odds} \times LR\]

lr_pos <- m$sensitivity / (1 - m$specificity)

pre <- 0.25
odds <- pre / (1 - pre) * lr_pos
odds / (1 + odds)

[1] 0.5309645


Works from any starting probability, in any setting (Deeks and Altman 2004).

title: Diagnostic Test Accuracy
text:
Summary

No reference standard, no accuracy
Sensitivity and specificity describe the test
Predictive values describe the population
Likelihood ratios connect the two
The threshold encodes what you are willing to get wrong

title: Sensitivity and Specificity
text:
In this chapter

Derive sensitivity and specificity and identify their denominators
Attach a confidence interval to each and explain why it is often wide
Use SnNout and SpPin correctly, and know when they mislead
Explain why these two measures alone cannot interpret a patient’s result


Sensitivity and specificity split the 2×2 table down its columns. Each asks about a group of patients defined by whether they have the disease.
Sensitivity asks: among patients who do have the disease, what proportion does the test detect?
\[
\text{Sensitivity} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}
\]
Specificity asks: among patients who do not have the disease, what proportion does the test correctly clear?
\[
\text{Specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}
\]
Both denominators are column totals. Neither involves the number of patients the test called positive, and neither depends on how common the disease is. This is the property that makes them portable between settings — and, as Chapter 3 shows, the property that makes them nearly useless at the bedside on their own.

title: Sensitivity and Specificity
text:
2 Computing them

sensitivity <- tab$tp / (tab$tp + tab$fn)
specificity <- tab$tn / (tab$tn + tab$fp)

c(sensitivity = round(sensitivity, 3),
  specificity = round(specificity, 3))

sensitivity specificity 
      0.961       0.717 


In our cohort the troponin threshold of 14 ng/L detects 96.1% of confirmed infarctions and correctly clears 71.7% of those without one.






Sanity check



74 true positives divided by 77 patients with confirmed MI gives 0.961. If a calculated sensitivity ever exceeds 1, you have used a row total as the denominator.

title: Sensitivity and Specificity
section: 3 A point estimate is not enough
text:
3 A point estimate is not enough
Both measures are proportions estimated from a sample, so both carry uncertainty. The denominator for sensitivity is only the diseased patients — here 77 of 600 — so the interval around it is usually much wider than the one around specificity.

1sens_ci <- dtx_ci(tab$tp, tab$tp + tab$fn)
spec_ci <- dtx_ci(tab$tn, tab$tn + tab$fp)

round(rbind(sensitivity = c(est = sensitivity, lower = sens_ci[1], upper = sens_ci[2]),
            specificity = c(est = specificity, lower = spec_ci[1], upper = spec_ci[2])), 3)


1

Wilson score intervals. Preferred to the normal approximation because these proportions sit close to 1 and the denominators are small — see (Newcombe 1998).




              est lower upper
sensitivity 0.961 0.892 0.987
specificity 0.717 0.677 0.754










Figure 1: Point estimates with 95% Wilson intervals. The interval for sensitivity is wider because it rests on far fewer patients.





Reporting sensitivity as a bare percentage hides this. A test described as “92% sensitive” from a study of 25 diseased patients is compatible with a true sensitivity below 75%.

title: Sensitivity and Specificity
text:
4 SnNout and SpPin
Two mnemonics from evidence-based medicine, useful when their conditions hold:

SnNout — with a highly Snsitive test, a Negative result rules the diagnosis out
SpPin — with a highly Specific test, a Positive result rules it in

The logic is sound. A test that almost never misses the disease produces few false negatives, so a negative result is informative.






Where these mnemonics fail



Both are shortcuts around Bayes’ theorem, and both quietly assume the pre-test probability is not extreme. A 99% sensitive test does not rule out a disease in a patient whose pre-test probability was 90% to begin with — a negative result leaves them well above the threshold at which you would act. Use the mnemonics to build intuition, not to make decisions. Chapter 3 gives the arithmetic that always works.

title: Sensitivity and Specificity
section: 5 Why neither answers your patient’s question
text:
5 Why neither answers your patient’s question
Your patient does not ask “if I had an infarction, would this test have caught it?” They ask “I have a positive result — do I have an infarction?”
That reverses the conditioning. Sensitivity is \(P(\text{test}^+ \mid \text{disease})\); the question asks for \(P(\text{disease} \mid \text{test}^+)\). These are different quantities and confusing them is the prosecutor’s fallacy (Altman and Bland 1994).
In our cohort sensitivity is 96.1%, but the probability that a patient with a positive troponin actually infarcted is 33.3% — a very different number, and it depends on something sensitivity deliberately ignores.

title: Sensitivity and Specificity
text:
6 Check yourself

A screening test has sensitivity 0.95 and specificity 0.80. It is moved from a hospital population to a community population where the disease is ten times rarer. What happens to the sensitivity?

It falls, because there are fewer cases to detect
It stays approximately the same, provided the spectrum of disease is similar
It rises, because there are fewer false positives
It cannot be calculated in the new setting


Sensitivity is conditional on having the disease, so changing how many people have it does not change the proportion detected. The caveat is real though: if the community cases are milder than the hospital cases, sensitivity can genuinely fall — that is spectrum bias, not a prevalence effect.



Which single change would most reduce the number of false negatives?

Lowering the troponin threshold below 14 ng/L
Raising the troponin threshold above 14 ng/L
Testing more patients
Using a stricter reference standard


Lowering the threshold calls more patients positive, so fewer diseased patients are missed: sensitivity rises. The price is more false positives and lower specificity. Chapter 4 traces that trade-off across every possible threshold.

title: References and Further Reading
text:
The BMJ “Diagnostic tests” series by Altman and Bland remains the clearest short introduction to the subject, and is worth reading in full before anything longer (Altman and Bland 1994a, 1994b; Deeks and Altman 2004).
For anyone appraising or designing a diagnostic accuracy study, STARD sets out what must be reported (Bossuyt et al. 2015) and QUADAS-2 gives the framework for judging risk of bias (Whiting et al. 2011). The clinical definitions used throughout come from the fourth universal definition of myocardial infarction (Thygesen et al. 2019). The interpretation of the area under the ROC curve follows Hanley and McNeil (Hanley and McNeil 1982), and the confidence intervals use the methods compared by Newcombe (Newcombe 1998).

title: References and Further Reading
text:
The BMJ “Diagnostic tests” series by Altman and Bland remains the clearest short introduction to the subject, and is worth reading in full before anything longer (Altman and Bland 1994a, 1994b; Deeks and Altman 2004).

The clinical definitions used throughout come from the fourth universal definition of myocardial infarction (Thygesen et al. 2019). title: References and Further Reading
text:
Suggested next steps
For teaching colleagues who want to extend this material:

Diagnostic meta-analysis — pooling sensitivity and specificity across studies requires bivariate models, because the two measures are negatively correlated through the threshold.
Multiple tests in sequence — how likelihood ratios combine when tests are conditionally independent, and what goes wrong when they are not.
Net benefit and decision curve analysis — a formal extension of the cost-weighting shown in Chapter 4.
Prediction models — calibration, discrimination and the difference between a good model and a useful one.

title: Self-Assessment
text: Work through these without looking back. Your score updates as you go; nothing is recorded or sent anywhere.

title: Self-Assessment
text:
1 Section A — building the table

A reference standard is best described as:

The test that is cheapest to perform
The best available method for determining whether the target condition is present
The test with the highest sensitivity
The result recorded in the patient’s notes


It is the comparator we are willing to treat as truth. It is rarely perfect, which is why “gold standard” has largely been abandoned as a term.



In a 2×2 table with the reference standard in columns, sensitivity is calculated using:

The top row
The left-hand column
The bottom row
The whole table


Sensitivity is TP / (TP + FN) — both cells of the disease-present column. Predictive values read across rows; sensitivity and specificity read down columns.



A study gives the reference standard only to patients whose index test was positive. This produces:

Partial verification bias, inflating sensitivity
Spectrum bias, deflating specificity
Incorporation bias, inflating specificity
No bias, provided the sample is large enough


Without reference-standard results in test-negative patients, the false-negative cell is incomplete and sensitivity is overstated. Common when the reference standard is invasive.

title: Self-Assessment
text:
2 Section B — calculating measures
Use the cohort figures: TP = 74, FP = 148, FN = 3, TN = 375. Enter answers as decimals to two places; the box turns teal when you are within tolerance.
Sensitivity is ? and specificity is ?.
The positive predictive value is ? and the prevalence in this cohort is ?.

Why is a Wilson interval preferred to the normal approximation for sensitivity?

It is easier to calculate by hand
It behaves properly when the proportion is near 1 or the denominator is small
It gives narrower intervals, which are more precise
It is required by the STARD statement


The normal approximation can produce intervals extending beyond 1, or absurdly narrow ones, exactly where diagnostic accuracy estimates usually sit. Narrower is not better if the coverage is wrong.



A test has sensitivity 0.80 and specificity 0.90. Its positive likelihood ratio is:

0.89
4.0
8.0
0.22


LR⁺ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) = 0.80 / 0.10 = 8.0. The 0.22 is the negative likelihood ratio, (1 − 0.80) / 0.90.

title: Self-Assessment
text:
3 Section C — prevalence and Bayes

Which quantities change when the same test is moved to a population where the disease is rarer?

Sensitivity and specificity
Positive and negative predictive value
Likelihood ratios
The area under the ROC curve


Sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios and AUC all describe the test and are independent of prevalence. Predictive values describe what a result means in a given population, and move with it.



A patient’s pre-test probability is 40%. A test with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.1 comes back negative. The post-test probability is closest to:

4%
6%
10%
25%


Pre-test odds = 0.4/0.6 = 0.667. Post-test odds = 0.667 × 0.1 = 0.0667. Probability = 0.0667/1.0667 = 0.063, about 6%. The intuitive answer of 4% comes from multiplying the probability directly, which is the error the odds conversion exists to prevent.



Screening a low-prevalence population with a highly accurate test typically produces:

Few false positives, because the test is accurate
Many false positives relative to true positives, because most people tested are healthy
Reduced sensitivity
An improved positive predictive value


The false positives come from the large healthy majority. Even a 1% false positive rate applied to hundreds of thousands of healthy people swamps the small number of genuine cases. This is the central difficulty in every screening programme.

title: Self-Assessment
text:
4 Section D — thresholds and ROC

Lowering a diagnostic threshold will:

Increase sensitivity and decrease specificity
Increase both sensitivity and specificity
Increase specificity and decrease sensitivity
Leave both unchanged but improve PPV


More patients are called positive, so fewer cases are missed and more healthy patients are wrongly flagged. Every point on an ROC curve is one such trade.



The area under the ROC curve represents:

The proportion of patients correctly classified
The probability that a random diseased patient scores higher than a random non-diseased patient
The best achievable sensitivity
Accuracy at the optimal threshold


It is a threshold-free measure of discrimination, not of accuracy. A test can have an excellent AUC and still be useless at the cut-off you actually use, or in the population you actually serve.



For a rule-out test in the emergency department, where a missed infarction is far worse than a false alarm, the threshold should be set to:

A low value, prioritising sensitivity
A high value, prioritising specificity
The Youden index optimum
The assay manufacturer’s stated cut-off


Youden weights the two errors equally, which is not the clinical reality here. When a false negative is many times more costly than a false positive, the optimum moves to a lower threshold — as the cost curves in Chapter 4 show.



A colleague reports that a new biomarker has “94% accuracy”. What is the most useful next question?

What was the sample size?
Was the study randomised?
What were the sensitivity, specificity and prevalence?
What was the AUC?


Overall accuracy is dominated by prevalence. In a population where 6% have the disease, a test that calls everyone negative achieves 94% accuracy while detecting nothing. Accuracy alone is close to uninterpretable without the components behind it.

title: Self-Assessment
text:
5 Where to go next
If several answers surprised you, the chapter each question came from is worth revisiting — Section C maps to Chapter 3 and Section D to Chapter 4. The glossary collects every term in one place, and the references point to the primary literature.

title: Diagnostic Test Accuracy
text:
A 58-year-old man arrives in the emergency department with chest pain. His high-sensitivity troponin comes back at 22 ng/L, above the laboratory cut-off. Does he have a myocardial infarction?
The test does not answer that question. It shifts a probability. How far it shifts, and from where, is what this course is about.
Everything below rests on one small table. In our teaching cohort of 600 patients presenting with chest pain, 77 were eventually confirmed to have had an infarction. Comparing the troponin result against that final diagnosis gives:
Two cells the test got right, in teal. Two it got wrong, in rose. Every measure in this course — sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, the ROC curve — is a ratio built from those four numbers. That colour convention holds on every page, so you can always see at a glance which part of the table a formula is reading.

In the table above, the 3 patients in the lower-left cell are those whose troponin was below the cut-off but who turned out to have had an infarction. What are they called?

What you need



The course reads perfectly well in a browser with no software installed. To run the code yourself you need R, RStudio and the knitr package. No other packages are required — everything uses base R.

title: The 2×2 Table
text:
In this chapter

Turn a continuous measurement into a binary test result
Build a 2×2 table against a reference standard
Name all four cells and both margins without hesitating
Recognise the three errors that most often corrupt such a table

title: The 2×2 Table
text:
1 The reference standard comes first
A diagnostic test is never assessed on its own. It is compared against something we are prepared to treat as the truth — the reference standard.1 For myocardial infarction that is the Fourth Universal Definition: a rise or fall in cardiac troponin together with clinical evidence of ischaemia (Thygesen et al. 2019).
This ordering matters. If you have no reference standard, you have no 2×2 table and no accuracy to measure — only agreement between two fallible measurements, which is a different question entirely.

section: 3 Turning a measurement into a result
text:
3 Turning a measurement into a result
Troponin is continuous. A 2×2 table needs a yes or a no. So we impose a threshold — here the conventional 99th-percentile upper reference limit of 14 ng/L.

1threshold <- 14
2cohort$test_positive <- cohort$troponin_ng_L >= threshold

3table(cohort$test_positive)


1

The cut-off, in ng/L. Changing this single number changes every measure in the course — which is the whole subject of Chapter 4.

2

>= produces TRUE or FALSE for each patient.

3

A quick sanity check before going further.





FALSE  TRUE 
  378   222 








The threshold is a decision, not a fact



Nothing in the biology of troponin makes 14 ng/L the right number. It is a choice about how willing we are to be wrong in each direction, and a different choice would give a different test. Treating a cut-off as though it were inherent to the assay is one of the commonest conceptual errors in diagnostic reasoning.

title: The 2×2 Table
text:
5 Reading the table
Learn these four names now; the rest of the course assumes them.




Table 2: The four cells and what each represents clinically.












Cell
Test
Disease
Clinical consequence




True positive (TP)
Positive
Present
Correctly identified; treatment begins


False positive (FP)
Positive
Absent
Unnecessary admission, further tests, anxiety


False negative (FN)
Negative
Present
Missed diagnosis; patient discharged untreated


True negative (TN)
Negative
Absent
Correctly reassured and discharged








The margins matter too. The row totals are how many patients the test called positive or negative. The column totals are how many actually had the disease — 77 of 600 here, a prevalence of 12.8%.

Which way round?
Convention puts the reference standard in columns and the test in rows. Sensitivity and specificity are then read down the columns, predictive values across the rows. If you fix that orientation in your mind now, you will never have to re-derive which denominator a formula wants.

title: The 2×2 Table
section: 6 Three ways this table goes wrong
text:
6 Three ways this table goes wrong






Partial verification bias





Only patients with a positive index test receive the reference standard. The FN and TN cells are then built from incomplete information, and sensitivity is inflated. Common wherever the reference standard is invasive, expensive or carries risk — coronary angiography being the obvious example here.









Incorporation bias





The index test is itself part of the reference standard. Troponin appears in the universal definition of MI, so a troponin-based index test is partly being compared against itself, and accuracy is overstated. Rarely avoidable; it must be declared.









Spectrum bias





Accuracy is estimated in a population unlike the one where the test will be used — florid inpatient cases versus undifferentiated primary-care presentations. Sensitivity and specificity are stable across prevalence but not across case mix, a distinction Chapter 3 returns to. The STARD statement exists largely to make these design features visible (Bossuyt et al. 2015).

title: The 2×2 Table
text:
7 Check yourself

A study enrols 500 patients. 60 have the disease. The test is positive in 48 of those 60, and positive in 35 of the remaining patients. How many true negatives are there?

12
35
405
452


Of the 440 patients without the disease, 35 tested positive, so 440 − 35 = 405 tested negative and did not have the disease. The 12 is the false-negative count (60 − 48), and 452 is the total number of negative tests (405 + 12).



A hospital introduces the same troponin assay in its outpatient chest-pain clinic, where far fewer patients turn out to have infarcted. Which of the following will change?

Sensitivity
Specificity
The positive predictive value
Nothing, provided the assay and cut-off are unchanged


Sensitivity and specificity are conditional on disease status and are unaffected by how common the disease is. Predictive values are conditional on the test result and depend directly on prevalence — which is why the same positive result means something different in the clinic than in resus. Chapter 3 works through the arithmetic.

title: The 2×2 Table
text:
8 What is next
You can now build the table. Chapter 2 turns it into the two measures that describe the test itself, and shows why neither one answers the question your patient is actually asking.

title: Glossary
text:
The four cells
True positive (TP) — test positive, disease present. Correct detection.
False positive (FP) — test positive, disease absent. A false alarm, leading to unnecessary investigation, treatment and anxiety. Sometimes called a type I error.
False negative (FN) — test negative, disease present. A missed diagnosis; usually the more dangerous error in acute medicine. Sometimes called a type II error.
True negative (TN) — test negative, disease absent. Correct reassurance.

title: Glossary
text:
Study design and bias
Reference standard — the best available method for establishing whether the target condition is present. Replaces the older term “gold standard”, which implied a perfection few reference standards have.
Index test — the test being evaluated.
Partial verification bias — the reference standard is applied only to patients with particular index test results, most often only the positives. The false-negative cell is then incomplete and sensitivity is inflated.
Incorporation bias — the index test forms part of the reference standard, so the test is partly compared against itself. Accuracy is overstated.
Spectrum bias — accuracy is estimated in a population whose severity mix differs from the population where the test will be used. Unlike prevalence effects, this genuinely changes sensitivity and specificity.
STARD — Standards for Reporting Diagnostic Accuracy studies, a checklist of items that must be reported for a reader to judge whether these biases are present (Bossuyt et al. 2015).
QUADAS-2 — a tool for assessing risk of bias in diagnostic accuracy studies included in a systematic review (Whiting et al. 2011).

title: Glossary
text:
Probability and inference
Pre-test probability — the probability of disease before the test result is known, based on history, examination and setting. Also called prior probability.
Post-test probability — the revised probability after incorporating the result. Also called posterior probability.
Odds — probability divided by its complement, \(p/(1-p)\). Likelihood ratios multiply odds, not probabilities, which is why the conversion step cannot be skipped.
Bayes’ theorem — the rule relating pre-test to post-test probability. In its practical clinical form: post-test odds = pre-test odds × likelihood ratio.
Prosecutor’s fallacy — confusing \(P(\text{result} \mid \text{disease})\) with \(P(\text{disease} \mid \text{result})\); that is, treating sensitivity as though it were the positive predictive value.
Wilson score interval — a confidence interval for a proportion that behaves well near 0 and 1 and with small denominators, unlike the normal approximation (Newcombe 1998).

title: Glossary
text:
Decision-making
Threshold (cut-off) — the value above which a continuous measurement is called positive. A decision about the relative cost of each error, not a property of the assay.
Decision threshold — the post-test probability at which management changes. A test is worth ordering only if a plausible result could carry the patient across one.
SnNout — with a highly sensitive test, a negative result helps rule the diagnosis out. Fails when the pre-test probability is high.
SpPin — with a highly specific test, a positive result helps rule it in. Fails when the pre-test probability is very low.
ROC curve — the plot of sensitivity against 1 − specificity across all possible thresholds (Hanley and McNeil 1982).
